concept.title: From a physics law to a running simulation
concept.intro: Every problem in Tensorizer follows the same 1 + 7 steps: tests first (step 0), then seven steps from picture to plot. Here they are for the simplest one: a pendulum swinging under gravity. Each step matches a file you can open, run and edit in the Problems tab.
concept.s0.title: Step 0: write the tests first
concept.s0.p1: Before any solver code, write down how you will know the answer is right. In `test.py` each test is a physical law the pendulum must obey: for a tiny swing the period is $2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$, the energy $\tfrac12 mL^2\dot\theta^2 + mgL(1-\cos\theta)$ stays constant, and a big swing is slower, exactly as the elliptic integral says.
concept.s0.p2: This is test-driven development (TDD): the tests fail at first, and you write steps 4–6 until they pass. The app runs `test.py` after every render and shows a green or red TDD light. It is recommended, not enforced, and it keeps an AI agent honest too: a change that breaks the physics turns the light red.
concept.s1.title: Start from the physical picture
concept.s1.p1: A point mass $m$ hangs on a light rod of length $L$. Gravity $g$ pulls it down; the only coordinate that matters is the angle $\theta$ from the vertical.
concept.s1.p2: Decide what you want to know before writing any equation: how does $\theta$ change in time, and does a big swing take longer than a small one?
concept.s2.title: Write the law in vector form
concept.s2.p1: Newton's second law along the arc of the swing, $m L\ddot\theta = -mg\sin\theta$, gives the equation of motion:
concept.s2.p2: It is nonlinear because of $\sin\theta$, so there is no simple formula for $\theta(t)$. A computer will march it forward in time instead. For small swings $\sin\theta\approx\theta$ and the familiar solution $\theta_0\cos(\sqrt{g/L}\,t)$ comes back.
concept.s3.title: Rewrite it in index (tensor) form
concept.s3.p1: Instead of one pendulum, release $B$ of them from different angles and give each an index $b$. The law becomes one statement about a whole tensor of angles:
concept.s3.p2: Read the indices like a spreadsheet: $\theta_b$ is a column of $B$ numbers. Nothing is summed here: each pendulum obeys the same law independently. In other problems a repeated index is summed (Einstein convention), e.g. $v_j v_j = \lvert v\rvert^2$, and that sum becomes one `torch.einsum` call.
concept.s4.title: Turn the quantities into tensors
concept.s4.p1: The state of every pendulum is its angle and angular velocity, so the whole system is one tensor $y$ of shape $(B, 2)$. A second-order equation becomes two first-order ones: $\dot\theta_b = \omega_b$ and $\dot\omega_b = -(g/L)\sin\theta_b$.
concept.s5.title: Write the law as a function
concept.s5.p1: `equation.py` is the translation step: each line of the index form becomes a line of PyTorch, applied to all pendulums at once. Comments carry the shapes so you can check them like units.
concept.s5.p2: The small-angle solution is an outer product (two indices, nothing summed), so it is written with einsum as `t,b->tb`:
concept.s6.title: Solve: march forward in time
concept.s6.p1: Fourth-order Runge–Kutta takes small steps $\Delta t$: it samples the right-hand side four times per step and combines them, with an error that shrinks like $\Delta t^4$. Because the state is a tensor, one RK4 step updates all $B$ pendulums together. On a GPU this is how thousands of simulations run in parallel.
concept.s7.title: Look at the result, and check it
concept.s7.p1: `plot.py` turns the trajectory tensor of shape $(T, B, 2)$ into an animation: each pendulum swings next to its dashed small-angle partner, and the big swings visibly fall behind.
concept.s7.p2: Never trust a simulation you have not checked. The tests compare against things we know exactly: energy $\tfrac12L^2\omega^2 + gL(1-\cos\theta)$ must stay constant, small swings must have period $2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$, and large swings must match the elliptic-integral formula.
concept.turn.title: Your turn
concept.turn.text: Open the pendulum, change the largest amplitude or gravity, tick Verbose output to watch every tensor shape go by, or edit `equation.py`: try replacing `sin(theta)` with `theta` and see the pendulums stay in step.

skills.title: The PyTorch toolbox behind every problem
skills.intro: The whole library is built from a handful of techniques. Learn them once and every problem becomes readable. Each card links to problems where you can see the technique in context and run it.
skills.tdd.title: Test first (TDD): physics as tests
skills.tdd.text: Step 0 of every problem is `test.py`: before writing the solver, state what any correct answer must satisfy, as a physical law: energy or momentum conserved, a limiting case that matches a known formula, a symmetry, or bounds such as $0 \le p \le 1$. Then write the code until the tests pass. The app runs `test.py` after every render and shows a green or red TDD light. It is recommended, not enforced, and it is also the best guard-rail for an AI agent: a change that breaks physics turns the light red.
skills.tensors.title: Tensors, shapes and devices
skills.tensors.text: Every physical quantity is a tensor with a shape you can say out loud: $B$ pendulums × 2 state variables is `(B, 2)`. Keep shapes in comments like units, and create tensors on one `device` so the same code runs on CPU or GPU.
skills.broadcasting.title: Broadcasting
skills.broadcasting.text: Combine tensors of different shapes without loops: a column `(A, 1)` against a row `(1, L)` fills an `(A, L)` table. Pairwise separations $r_{ab} = x_b - x_a$ of $N$ bodies are one subtraction.
skills.einsum.title: einsum = index notation
skills.einsum.text: `torch.einsum` is the Einstein convention typed out: name each index, repeated indices are summed. $v_j v_j$ is `'bj,bj->b'`, a matrix acting on vectors $M_{ij}y_j$ is `'ij,rj->ri'`, a cross product $\varepsilon_{ijk}v_jB_k$ uses the Levi-Civita tensor.
skills.batching.title: Batching many simulations
skills.batching.text: Add a batch index instead of a Python loop: launch angles, amplitudes, isotopes or receptor variants become one more axis, and every operation handles them together. On a GPU this is where the speed comes from.
skills.rk4.title: Time stepping (RK4)
skills.rk4.text: Write the law as $\dot y = f(y, t)$ and march forward. Classical Runge–Kutta samples $f$ four times per step with error $\propto \Delta t^4$; because $y$ is a tensor, one step updates the whole system.
skills.linalg.title: Linear algebra: solve and eigh
skills.linalg.text: Many problems are a matrix equation once discretised: $L_{ij}\phi_j = -\rho_i$ is `torch.linalg.solve`, and normal modes or quantum levels $H_{ij}\psi_j = E\,\psi_i$ come from `torch.linalg.eigh`.
skills.stencils.title: Finite differences, stencils and conv2d
skills.stencils.text: A derivative on a grid is a small stencil; the Laplacian $\partial_i\partial_i u$ is the kernel $[[0,1,0],[1,-4,1],[0,1,0]]/h^2$. `conv2d` applies it everywhere at once, and the time step must respect the CFL condition.
skills.fft.title: Spectral methods with FFT
skills.fft.text: In Fourier space a derivative is a multiplication by $ik$. Free evolution, dispersion and the kinetic step of the Schrödinger equation become element-wise products between two FFTs.
skills.autograd.title: Autograd for physics
skills.autograd.text: PyTorch can differentiate any code: forces from a potential, the mass matrix of a Lagrangian, a tidal tensor $-\partial_i\partial_j\Phi$, or Christoffel symbols from a metric $g_{\mu\nu}$, with no derivatives by hand.
skills.complex.title: Complex tensors and quantum states
skills.complex.text: Wavefunctions and fields are complex: use `torch.complex128`, `.conj()` and phases $e^{-iE_nt}$. Multi-qubit states are tensors $\psi_{ab}$, and gates act on them with einsum.

flow.title: Tensor dataflow: how the computer actually runs it
flow.intro: The first tab turns a law into tensor code. This one opens the box: what a tensor is in memory, why one line of `einsum` beats a Python loop, what a GPU does differently, and how frameworks record the computation as a dataflow graph to differentiate and speed it up. The ideas are the same in PyTorch, JAX, MLX and TensorFlow; we show PyTorch and a table of the others.
flow.name: Why “dataflow”? Tensors flow through a graph of operations: each node is a kernel, each edge a tensor. That picture, not any one library, is what the rest of this page explains.
flow.s1.title: A tensor is a block of memory with a shape
flow.s1.p1: A tensor is one flat buffer of numbers plus a little metadata: its **dtype** (for example float32, 4 bytes each), its **shape** and its **strides**, the step in memory to the next element along each axis. Element $x_{ij}$ of a $(2, 3)$ tensor sits at offset $3i + j$, so the strides are $(3, 1)$.
flow.s1.p2: Many operations only change the metadata. A transpose swaps the strides to $(1, 3)$; a slice moves the start offset and can change the shape and strides (`x[:, ::2]` doubles the column stride); none of these copies a number. Advanced indexing with a list or a mask (`x[[0, 1, 1]]`) does copy. The **device** says where the buffer lives: CPU memory or GPU memory. Step through the lab below and watch which memory cell each element reads.
flow.s1.p3: Zero-copy has a cost later. A non-contiguous tensor is read in jumps through memory, which breaks cache-line locality on the CPU and the GPU: each cache line fetched brings neighbours the next step doesn't use. When a kernel needs a contiguous buffer, `.contiguous()` is the moment the real copy happens.
flow.s2.title: Vectorise: one kernel instead of a loop
flow.s2.p1: A Python loop pays interpreter overhead for every element. A tensor operation hands the whole buffer to compiled **kernels**, which stream through memory with SIMD instructions (several numbers per CPU instruction) and many threads. One expression is not always one kernel: `a * b + c` may launch one kernel per operation, each reading and writing memory (section 6 shows how fusion merges them). Batching all cases into one tensor still pays: a few kernel launches instead of a loop over every element.
flow.s2.p2: **Broadcasting** is free in memory: `expand` gives a missing axis stride $0$, so the same numbers are reused instead of copied. `x[:, None, :] - x[None, :, :]` builds all $N^2$ pair separations as a $(N, N, 3)$ result from an $(N, 3)$ input.
flow.mem.title: Broadcasting saves the inputs, not the output
flow.mem.p1: The views `x[None, :, :]` and `x[:, None, :]` copy nothing, but the result $D_{abi} = X_{bi} - X_{ai}$ is a new tensor of $N \times N \times 3$ numbers: $12 N^2$ bytes in float32. That is 12 MB for a thousand particles, 1.2 GB for ten thousand and 120 GB for a hundred thousand, before any intermediate results or gradients. Slide $N$ below.
flow.mem.p2: So vectorisation is not about building the biggest tensor. Large problems process the pairs in chunks, keep only near neighbours (neighbour lists, sparse tensors) or use a fused kernel that never stores $D$ at all. The aim is a data layout and a sequence of operations that fit the hardware's memory.
flow.s3.title: What a GPU does differently
flow.s3.p1: A GPU runs thousands of lightweight threads at once, each handling a few elements of the same kernel, and its memory is several times faster than CPU memory. Big element-wise operations and matrix products on large batches are where it wins.
flow.s3.p2: It has fixed costs too. Launching a kernel takes microseconds, so a time loop of thousands of tiny steps on a few numbers can be faster on the CPU. Copying between CPU and GPU memory is slow: create tensors on the device once and keep them there. GPU work is asynchronous, so call `torch.cuda.synchronize()` before timing.
flow.s4.title: Contractions become matrix products
flow.s4.p1: `einsum` states a tensor contraction declaratively: which indices are summed and which are kept. Depending on the contraction pattern, the shapes and strides and the backend, it may be lowered to an optimised matrix multiplication (GEMM), a batched matrix multiplication or other kernels. Writing the index form as `einsum` keeps the mathematics exact and leaves that choice to the library; it does not promise the fastest kernel.
flow.s4.p2: Precision is a numerical modelling decision, not merely a hardware setting. float64 has about 16 significant digits, float32 about 7. Many consumer GPUs have far lower float64 than float32 throughput (data-centre GPUs much less so, and real speed also depends on memory traffic), and Apple's MPS has no float64 at all. Long time integrations, ill-conditioned matrices and cancellation can need float64 where float32 looks fine at first; Tensorizer's conservation tests are one way to find out.
flow.s5.title: The dataflow graph: gradients and speed
flow.s5.p1: While a computation runs, the framework records each operation and its inputs: a **dataflow graph** from parameters to result. Reverse-mode automatic differentiation walks the graph backwards applying the chain rule and gives the gradient of one number with respect to every input, typically for a small constant multiple of the forward cost; it has to keep intermediate results for the backward pass, so memory is often the real limit. That is how the Lagrangian, PINN and inverse-design problems get forces and gradients without writing derivatives.
flow.s5.p2: The same graph can be **compiled**: neighbouring element-wise operations are fused into one kernel so intermediate results never touch memory. PyTorch does it with `torch.compile`, JAX with `jit` (XLA), TensorFlow with `tf.function`; MLX is lazy and builds the graph until a value is needed. Eager code is easier to read and debug; compiled code is faster for long runs.
flow.s5.p3: Fusion pays because modern chips compute far faster (FLOPs) than they move data (memory bandwidth). For $A + B \times C$ the bottleneck is usually not the multiply-add but carrying the numbers from GPU memory into registers. Fusion keeps the data in registers for every operation and **writes the result back to memory only once**.
flow.s5.p4: Autograd differentiates exactly what you wrote, nothing more. In the code below $\phi = -GM/r$ is the potential per unit mass, so $-\nabla\phi$ is an acceleration; the force on a mass $m$ comes from the potential energy $U = -GMm/r$ as $\mathbf F = -\nabla U$. Naming the physical quantity correctly is still the physicist's job.
flow.s6.title: Same ideas, different frameworks
flow.s6.p1: The vocabulary changes, the principles don't. Writing the law in index notation keeps a problem portable: the `einsum` string is identical everywhere.
flow.s7.title: What Tensorizer does with all this
flow.s7.p1: Every problem builds its tensors once on `device()` (CUDA, MPS or CPU, chosen in the Backend panel), batches many cases along one axis, writes the physics as `einsum` and broadcasting, and uses float64 where a conservation law must hold to many digits. Small problems run well on a laptop CPU; the batched ones scale to a GPU unchanged.

loops.title: For loop vs tensor: why vectorised code is faster
loops.intro: The same physics can be written as a Python `for` loop over every element, or as one tensor expression over all of them at once. Both give the same numbers, but the tensor version is often 10 to 1000 times faster. Below are six everyday examples side by side, each timed on a real machine.
loops.why.title: Why the loop is slow
loops.why.interp: **Interpreter overhead.** Every pass of a Python loop looks up names, checks types and wraps each float in an object: tens of nanoseconds of bookkeeping for a single multiply-add. A tensor operation pays that cost once, then runs a compiled C++ or CUDA kernel over all $N$ elements.
loops.why.memory: **Memory layout and SIMD.** A tensor stores its numbers side by side in memory, so the CPU streams them through its caches and processes 4 to 16 at a time with vector (SIMD) instructions. A Python list holds pointers to float objects scattered around memory.
loops.why.batch: **Batching.** Many independent copies of a problem (pendulums, particles, grid cells) become one extra tensor dimension, so a single call advances all of them, and the work is spread over every CPU core.
loops.why.gpu: **GPU.** The same tensor code runs on a GPU after `.to("cuda")`, where thousands of cores work in parallel. A Python loop cannot follow it there.
loops.howto: Each card shows the loop and the tensor version of the same calculation; both return the same result (checked with `torch.allclose` in float64). The bars show the measured speed-up $t_\text{loop} / t_\text{tensor}$ on a log scale, for three problem sizes.
loops.range: Error bar: spread over the passes.
loops.dot.title: Sum of squares / dot product
loops.dot.text: $s = \sum_i x_i y_i$: one multiply-add per loop pass, against a single call to `torch.dot`, an optimised BLAS kernel. With `y = x` it is the sum of squares.
loops.pairwise.title: Pairwise distances of $N$ particles
loops.pairwise.text: Broadcasting `x[:, None] - x[None, :]` builds all $N^2$ separations $\mathbf{r}_{ij}$ at once instead of a double loop: the core of every N-body force calculation.
loops.matmul.title: Matrix multiply
loops.matmul.text: $C_{ij} = \sum_k A_{ik} B_{kj}$ takes $n^3$ multiply-adds; `A @ B` hands them to a cache-blocked, multithreaded BLAS routine, so the gap grows fastest here.
loops.pendulum.title: One RK4 step for $B$ pendulums
loops.pendulum.text: The state of all pendulums is one $(B, 2)$ tensor, so each RK4 stage is a handful of tensor operations instead of $B$ separate scalar updates.
loops.diffusion.title: A diffusion step on an $n \times n$ grid
loops.diffusion.text: The five-point Laplacian $u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j} + u_{i,j+1} + u_{i,j-1} - 4u_{ij}$ is four shifted slices of the same grid, with no index loops; `conv2d` with a 3 × 3 kernel does the same.
loops.mc_pi.title: Monte Carlo $\pi$
loops.mc_pi.text: Test all $N$ darts against $x^2 + y^2 \le 1$ in one comparison and take the mean: $\pi \approx 4 \times$ the fraction inside the quarter circle.

loops.hw.label: Hardware acceleration
loops.hw.matmul: Dedicated matrix-multiply (GEMM) units: Tensor Cores, Matrix Cores, AMX, XMX, SME, TPU MXU. A Python loop can never reach them; see the table below.
loops.hw.table.title: Dedicated matrix units by vendor
loops.hw.matmul.why: They only help when the work is one big matrix product: a Python loop can never reach them. A @ B and einsum dispatch to cuBLAS, oneDNN or Accelerate, which use them.
loops.hw.pairwise: Distance matrices as GEMM. ‖xᵢ − xⱼ‖² = ‖xᵢ‖² + ‖xⱼ‖² − 2 xᵢ·xⱼ turns all distances into one matrix product (torch.cdist does this for large inputs), so they can use the matrix-multiply units of the GPU or CPU.
loops.hw.diffusion: Convolutions as GEMM. The five-point stencil is a 3 × 3 convolution (conv2d); cuDNN and oneDNN often rewrite convolutions as one matrix product (im2col), so they can run on the same matrix-multiply units.
loops.hw.dot: Vector units. SIMD fused multiply-add (AVX2 / AVX-512 on x86, NEON on Arm) handles 4 to 16 numbers per instruction; GPUs sum across threads with warp-level shuffle instructions.
loops.hw.mc_pi: Parallel random numbers. On a GPU, PyTorch and cuRAND draw random numbers with the counter-based Philox generator: every thread computes its own part of the stream directly, with no shared sequential state.
loops.fine.title: When a loop is fine
loops.fine.text: Time stepping is inherently sequential: step $t + 1$ needs step $t$, so the loop over time stays. What goes is the loop over everything else: particles, pendulums, grid points, rays, samples. Turn those into tensor dimensions and keep one short Python loop over $t$; its overhead is then paid once per step, not once per element.
loops.fine.small: Very small sizes are the other exception. For a few hundred elements the fixed cost of launching a tensor kernel dominates and the speed-up shrinks, as the smallest sizes in the bars show; on a GPU the smallest cases can even be slower than on the CPU.

blas.title: BLAS: the library under every matrix multiply
blas.intro: When you write `A @ B`, `torch.linalg.solve` or `np.dot`, the arithmetic is done by a BLAS (Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms) library: a few dozen routines with a fixed interface, implemented separately and tuned for each family of processors. Which BLAS you have decides how fast your code runs, and in the last few bits, what numbers it returns.
blas.howto: Below: what BLAS is and why the matrix-matrix routine is special, the main libraries, how to find out which one your PyTorch and NumPy use, why results differ slightly between machines, and matrix-multiply throughput measured on this project's machine.
blas.what.title: What BLAS is
blas.what.text: BLAS groups its routines in three levels by the shapes involved. What separates them is the **arithmetic intensity**: floating-point operations per value moved to and from memory. Level 1 and Level 2 do $O(1)$ operations per value, so they run at the speed of memory; Level 3 (GEMM, general matrix multiply) does $O(n)$ operations per value, so it can keep the arithmetic units busy.
blas.what.fastTitle: Why GEMM gets close to the peak
blas.what.blocking: **Cache blocking and packing.** The matrices are cut into tiles that fit in the L1, L2 and L3 caches and copied (packed) into contiguous buffers, so every value loaded from main memory is reused many times before it is evicted.
blas.what.kernel: **SIMD micro-kernel.** At the centre is a small hand-written kernel that keeps a block of $C$ in vector registers and updates it with fused multiply-add (FMA) instructions, 8 to 16 numbers per instruction (AVX2, AVX-512, NEON, SVE).
blas.what.threads: **Threads.** Independent tiles of $C$ go to different cores; on a GPU, cuBLAS spreads them over thousands of threads (and Tensor Cores where the precision allows).
blas.eq.roofNote: $P$: peak compute (GFLOP/s), $\beta$: memory bandwidth (GB/s), $I$: arithmetic intensity (FLOP/byte).
blas.roof.caption: The roofline idea, with illustrative numbers ($P$ = 400 GFLOP/s, $\beta$ = 40 GB/s). Left of the ridge, the speed of memory sets the limit; right of it, the arithmetic units do. Vector and matrix–vector routines sit far to the left; GEMM moves right as $n$ grows.
blas.libs.title: BLAS libraries
blas.libs.text: All of them implement the same interface (the names `sgemm`, `dgemm`, `saxpy`, … come from the 1979–1990 reference specification), so a program can be linked against any of them. They differ in the hardware they are tuned for, their licence and how they reach PyTorch and NumPy. The library names link to the official documentation.
blas.libs.table.title: Libraries at a glance
blas.lib.netlib.notes: The reference implementation that defines the interface; correct but not tuned.
blas.lib.netlib.via: Not used for speed; the API every other library implements.
blas.lib.openblas.notes: Descendant of GotoBLAS2; hand-tuned kernels per CPU, chosen at run time.
blas.lib.openblas.via: NumPy and SciPy wheels on PyPI; conda-forge `libblas=*=*openblas`.
blas.lib.mkl.hw: x86-64 CPUs (and Intel GPUs via SYCL)
blas.lib.mkl.notes: Also LAPACK, FFT, sparse BLAS and random numbers.
blas.lib.aocl.notes: AMD's tuned fork of BLIS, part of AMD Optimizing CPU Libraries (AOCL).
blas.lib.aocl.via: Linked as the system BLAS in custom builds.
blas.lib.blis.notes: A framework: only a small micro-kernel is written per CPU, the blocking around it is generic.
blas.lib.accelerate.hw: Apple CPUs (M-series: also the AMX matrix units)
blas.lib.accelerate.notes: Apple's framework: BLAS, LAPACK, vDSP; ships with macOS.
blas.lib.accelerate.via: NumPy 2.x wheels for macOS 14+ on Apple silicon; conda-forge `libblas=*=*accelerate`.
blas.lib.cublas.notes: Uses Tensor Cores for the precisions they support; cuBLASLt is the lightweight API with fused epilogues (bias, activation) and mixed precision.
blas.lib.cublas.via: Every `matmul` on a CUDA tensor; CuPy.
blas.lib.rocblas.notes: AMD's counterparts of cuBLAS and cuBLASLt.
blas.lib.rocblas.via: PyTorch ROCm builds (tensors on the `cuda` device).
blas.lib.onednn.notes: Not a BLAS: deep-learning primitives (convolution, matmul, normalisation) with kernels generated at run time; formerly MKL-DNN.
blas.lib.onednn.via: PyTorch CPU convolutions and some linear / matmul paths (`torch.backends.mkldnn`).
blas.libs.lapack: **LAPACK** sits on top of BLAS: solving linear systems, LU, Cholesky, QR, eigenvalues and SVD, written so that most of the work is Level 3 BLAS calls. `torch.linalg.solve`, `eigh` and `svd` on the CPU call the LAPACK in the same library (here `LAPACK_INFO=mkl`); on NVIDIA GPUs PyTorch uses cuSOLVER and MAGMA instead.
blas.libs.sparse: **Sparse matrices** (mostly zeros) need different routines: cuSPARSE on NVIDIA GPUs, the sparse BLAS in oneMKL on the CPU; `torch.sparse` reaches them.
blas.which.title: Which BLAS am I using?
blas.which.text: PyTorch and NumPy each report how they were built. In PyTorch, look for `BLAS_INFO` and `LAPACK_INFO` in the build settings, an "Intel(R) oneAPI Math Kernel Library" line (MKL) and an "MKL-DNN" / oneDNN line; NumPy lists its `blas` and `lapack` dependencies.
blas.which.threadsText: Each library has its own thread pool, sized at load time from an environment variable, so set it before Python starts: `OMP_NUM_THREADS` (OpenMP, also read by PyTorch), `MKL_NUM_THREADS`, `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS`. Inside a running program, `torch.set_num_threads(n)` resizes PyTorch's pool (and MKL's, in an MKL build). One thread per physical core is usually best; more threads than cores slows GEMM down.
blas.which.project: **This project.** The default environment uses conda-forge's `pytorch 2.14.1` CPU build `cpu_mkl`: `BLAS_INFO=mkl`, `LAPACK_INFO=mkl`, Intel oneMKL 2026.1, MKL-DNN (oneDNN) 3.12, OpenMP, CPU capability AVX2, and 6 threads on this 6-core machine. NumPy 2.5.4 reaches the same MKL through conda-forge's switchable `libblas` package (build `*_mkl`); `numpy.show_config()` only shows that package's generic name, `blas 3.9.0`, so `pixi list libblas` tells you which implementation is installed. The `cuda` environment (`pytorch 2.13.0`, build `cuda128_mkl`) uses MKL on the CPU and cuBLAS 12.8 on the GPU. The Linux lock file pins the same `*_mkl` builds.
blas.repro.title: Same code, slightly different numbers
blas.repro.text: Floating-point addition is not associative: $(a + b) + c$ and $a + (b + c)$ can differ in the last bit, because every addition rounds. A matrix product is millions of additions, and the order in which a BLAS library adds them depends on its tile sizes, its SIMD width (8 or 16 partial sums kept side by side), whether it uses FMA, how the work is split across threads, and the hardware. Change any of those and the last bits of the result change; none of the answers is more correct than the others.
blas.repro.measured: Measured here for a {n} × {n} float32 product: 1 thread and {threads} threads gave bit-for-bit identical results (MKL splits the rows and columns of $C$ between threads, not the sums), but the CPU and the GPU differed by up to {diff} in entries as large as about 23, a few parts in $10^7$: ordinary float32 rounding.
blas.repro.tol: So compare floating-point results with a tolerance that fits the precision: float32 keeps about 7 significant digits (machine epsilon $\approx 1.2 \times 10^{-7}$), and the error of a sum grows with the number of terms. Scale the tolerance to the size of the values when they are large.
blas.repro.det: On one machine with one software version, PyTorch can be asked for repeatable results. This removes run-to-run variation (from atomics and autotuned kernel choice on the GPU); it does not make two different BLAS libraries or two different processors agree.
blas.repro.ci.title: A worked example from this project's own tests
blas.repro.ci.text: Two tests passed on Windows and failed in continuous integration on Linux. Both environments use conda-forge's MKL builds, but a different operating-system build on a different cloud CPU means different kernels and a different summation order:
blas.repro.ci.hopfield: **Hopfield network.** Its energy must never increase during recall, and the test asserted every step change $\Delta E \le 10^{-5}$. With $|E| \sim 10^2$ in float32, a single rounding is already about $10^2 \times 6 \times 10^{-8} \approx 6 \times 10^{-6}$, and a few of them add up past $10^{-5}$. Fix: a tolerance relative to the energy, $\Delta E \le 10^{-6} \max |E|$.
blas.repro.ci.batched: **Batched vs alone.** A script that trains several models side by side in one batch checks that each model's loss curve matches the same model trained alone. In float32 the batched reductions add in a different order, and `rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-6` was tighter than float32 rounding over a training run. Fix: `rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-4`.
blas.repro.ci.lesson: Neither test was wrong about the physics or the model; their tolerances assumed one particular summation order. A test of float32 code should allow float32 rounding.

blas.bench.text: Throughput $2n^3 / t$ of `A @ B` for $n \times n$ matrices, on the CPU (MKL, float32 and float64, 1 thread and all threads) and on the GPU (cuBLAS). Small matrices are dominated by fixed costs (call overhead, starting threads, launching a GPU kernel); from a few hundred upwards GEMM approaches its plateau. Every configuration first had to agree with a float64 reference (`torch.allclose`).
blas.chart.range: Lines: median of the passes; error bar: spread over the passes; dashed: estimated peak (see below).
blas.bench.observe: At $n$ = 2048 the CPU reaches roughly 45 % of its estimated all-core peak and about two thirds of its single-core peak; float64 runs at about half the float32 rate, as the SIMD lanes hold half as many numbers. The GTX 1080 Ti reaches about 10 TFLOP/s in float32 but only about 0.35 TFLOP/s in float64: consumer Pascal cards run float64 at 1/32 of the float32 rate, so for float64 work this GPU is only about twice as fast as the 6-core CPU.

maths.title: Tensor maths, Penrose notation and the roofline model
maths.intro: Every program on this site boils down to a few ideas: arrays of numbers with named directions, a rule for multiplying them, a way of drawing that rule, and a reason why some of those multiplications run a hundred times faster than others. This page builds them up one at a time.
maths.feynman: **How the page is written.** Richard Feynman's test of understanding was whether he could explain something simply. So each section goes in the same order: first **in plain words**, then **a picture from everyday life**, then **the precise statement**, and finally **a tiny example** you can check by hand. No word of jargon is used before it has been earned.
maths.tensor.title: What a tensor is
maths.tensor.plain: A tensor is a box of numbers laid out along a few directions. The number of directions is its **rank** (or order): a single number has rank 0, a list rank 1, a table rank 2, a stack of tables rank 3, and so on. How long the box is in each direction is its **shape**. To pick out one number you name one position per direction: that position is an **index**.
maths.tensor.analogy: Think of addresses. In a village, a house number is enough (rank 1). In a block of flats you need floor and door (rank 2). In a city of tower blocks you need building, floor and door (rank 3). The shape says how many buildings, floors and doors there are; each flat is one component; the whole city is the tensor.
maths.tensor.precise: A rank-$r$ tensor in $n$ dimensions has $n^r$ components $T_{i_1 \dots i_r}$, one per choice of indices. The components depend on the coordinate system, the tensor itself does not: if the axes are rotated by a matrix $R$, a vector's components change as $v'_i = R_{ij} v_j$ and a matrix's as $A'_{ij} = R_{ik} R_{jl} A_{kl}$, with one factor of $R$ per index. In code the word tensor usually means just the array (shape and numbers), without the rule.
maths.tensor.updown: **Index up or down?** Measure a stick with a ruler marked in metres, then with one in centimetres: the number goes up 100 times because the unit went down. Components that behave like this are called contravariant and are written with an upper index, $v^i$ (displacements, velocities). Now count how many contour lines of a hill you cross per unit of distance: switch to centimetres and the count per unit goes down 100 times, the same way as the unit. Those are covariant, written with a lower index, $w_i$ (gradients). Pairing one upper with one lower index, $w_i v^i$, gives a number that does not care about the unit at all. With ordinary perpendicular axes of equal length the two kinds coincide, which is why array code never writes an index up.
maths.tensor.example: A colour photo of $480 \times 640$ pixels is a rank-3 tensor of shape $(480, 640, 3)$: row, column and colour channel, $921\,600$ numbers in all. A batch of 32 such photos adds a fourth index, shape $(32, 480, 640, 3)$. `x.ndim` gives the rank, `x.shape` the shape.
maths.tensor.fig: Rank = the number of indices = how many directions you must name to find one number.
maths.einsum.title: Einstein summation and contraction
maths.einsum.plain: Many formulas multiply numbers that share an index and then add up the products. Einstein noticed that he kept writing a summation sign over exactly those indices, so he stopped writing it: an index that appears twice in a term is summed over. Adding up over a shared index like this is called a **contraction**.
maths.einsum.analogy: A shopping receipt: quantities $q_i$ and prices $p_i$, one of each per item $i$. The total is $q_i p_i$: multiply item by item and add. The index $i$ is used up, because the total no longer belongs to any one item. That is a contraction.
maths.einsum.precise: In $C_{ik} = A_{ij} B_{jk}$ the index $j$ appears twice and is summed (a dummy index); $i$ and $k$ appear once and survive (free indices) and become the indices of the result. The free indices must be the same on both sides of an equation. The dot product, the matrix–vector product, the matrix product and the trace are all one operation, contraction, with different indices.
maths.einsum.example: With $A = \begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ the trace is $A_{ii} = 1 + 4 = 5$, and $(AA)_{11} = A_{1j}A_{j1} = 1\cdot 1 + 2\cdot 3 = 7$. `torch.einsum` takes the indices as letters; a letter missing after the arrow is summed, so `torch.einsum("ii->", A)` returns 5.
maths.einsum.fig: A matrix product: row $i$ of $A$ meets column $k$ of $B$, and the shared index $j$ is summed away.
maths.penrose.title: Penrose graphical notation
maths.penrose.plain: Index formulas become hard to read once there are many tensors. In 1971 Roger Penrose proposed drawing them instead: each tensor is a shape, and each index is a line, or leg, sticking out of it. A leg joined to another leg is a summed index; a leg left dangling is a free index. The number of dangling legs is the rank of the result.
maths.penrose.analogy: Think of gadgets with cables, one cable per index. Plugging two cables together means: sum over that index. Whatever cables are still loose at the end are the indices of the answer. You never have to write a summation; the wiring is the formula.
maths.penrose.precise: A vector is a node with one leg, a matrix a node with two, a rank-$r$ tensor a node with $r$ legs. Joining legs contracts those indices. Two diagrams side by side with nothing joined form the outer (tensor) product. A leg joined back to the same tensor is a trace, a loop. A bare line is the identity $\delta_{ij}$: it just passes the index along. Only the wiring matters, so nodes may be slid and bent along the wires as long as each leg stays on its slot. That is why $\operatorname{tr}(AB) = \operatorname{tr}(BA)$ is obvious in a picture: both are one loop through $A$ and $B$, and a loop has no start.
maths.penrose.example: Matrix–vector: draw $A$ with legs $i$ and $j$ and $v$ with leg $j$, then join the two $j$ legs. One leg, $i$, is left, so the answer is a vector, $w_i = A_{ij} v_j$. Join a vector $u$ onto the leg $i$ as well and nothing dangles: $u_i A_{ij} v_j$ is a single number. A long chain of rank-3 tensors, each joined to its neighbours and with one free leg each, is a matrix product state (MPS): it stores a tensor of $d^N$ numbers as $N$ small pieces, the starting point of tensor networks in quantum physics and of tensor-train compression in machine learning.
maths.penrose.fig.basic: Building blocks: the rank is the number of legs; a plain line is the identity.
maths.penrose.fig.ops: Joining legs contracts an index; side by side is the outer product; a loop is a trace.
maths.penrose.fig.trace: $\operatorname{tr}(AB) = \operatorname{tr}(BA)$: the same loop, read from another starting point.
maths.penrose.fig.mps: A matrix product state: $N$ small tensors instead of one tensor with $d^N$ numbers.
maths.topo.title: Operator topology: the order of the work
maths.topo.plain: A program that computes with tensors is a network of operators: each node does one operation (multiply, add, apply ReLU, sum) and each edge carries a tensor from one operation to the next. The shapes on the edges must fit, like the diameters of pipes. The same result can often be reached along different routes through the network, and the routes can cost very different amounts of work.
maths.topo.analogy: Cooking for a party: you can chop all the onions first and then fry them in one pan, or chop and fry them one at a time. The dish is the same; the time is not. Multiplying matrices is similar: the answer $ABC$ does not depend on where the brackets go (associativity), but the amount of work does.
maths.topo.precise: Multiplying an $a \times b$ matrix by a $b \times c$ matrix takes $abc$ multiplications (and as many additions: $2abc$ FLOPs). For shapes $a \times b$, $b \times c$ and $c \times d$, the orders $(AB)C$ and $A(BC)$ give the same matrix but cost $abc + acd$ and $bcd + abd$. For a chain the cheapest order is found by a short dynamic programme; for a general tensor network the search is NP-hard and libraries use greedy or exhaustive heuristics, such as `opt_einsum`, which `torch.einsum` uses for three or more operands when the package is installed (`torch.backends.opt_einsum`).
maths.topo.example: Take $A$ of shape $10 \times 100$, $B$ of $100 \times 5$ and $C$ of $5 \times 50$. $(AB)C$: $10 \cdot 100 \cdot 5 = 5\,000$ multiplications give a $10 \times 5$ matrix, then $10 \cdot 5 \cdot 50 = 2\,500$ more. $A(BC)$: $100 \cdot 5 \cdot 50 = 25\,000$ for a $100 \times 50$ matrix, then $10 \cdot 100 \cdot 50 = 50\,000$. The same answer for ten times the work. Rule of thumb: contract first where the intermediate result comes out small.
maths.topo.fig: A two-layer neural network as an operator graph: nodes are operations, edges carry tensors labelled with their shapes ($B$ = batch size).
maths.roof.title: Arithmetic intensity and the roofline model
maths.roof.plain: A processor does two jobs: arithmetic, and fetching numbers from memory to do the arithmetic on. Today arithmetic is cheap and fetching is expensive. So the speed of a calculation is set by whichever runs out first, the arithmetic units or the memory pipe. The ratio that decides it is the **arithmetic intensity**: how many floating-point operations you do for each byte you fetch.
maths.roof.analogy: A kitchen with a fast chef and a slow delivery van. If every dish needs a fresh van-load of ingredients (a salad: chop and serve), the chef stands waiting for the van; the kitchen is limited by delivery, memory-bound. If a few ingredients become an elaborate meal, the van keeps up easily and the chef is the limit, compute-bound. The roofline is a picture of this: a slope where the van limits, a flat roof where the chef does.
maths.roof.precise: With peak arithmetic rate $P$ (FLOP/s), memory bandwidth $\beta$ (byte/s) and a kernel's arithmetic intensity $I$ (FLOP/byte), the attainable rate is $P_\text{att} = \min(P,\ \beta I)$ (Williams, Waterman and Patterson, 2009). On log–log axes this is a slanted line rising up to the ridge point $I^* = P/\beta$, then a flat roof. Kernels left of the ridge are memory-bound, kernels right of it compute-bound.
maths.roof.ops: Where common operations sit (float32, 4 bytes per number, each operand read once and the result written once): element-wise $z = x + y$ does 1 FLOP per 12 bytes, $I = 1/12$; a dot product does $2n$ FLOPs on $8n$ bytes, $I = 1/4$; matrix–vector is about $1/2$. None of these grows with $n$, so they are memory-bound on every machine. Matrix–matrix does $2n^3$ FLOPs on $3n^2$ numbers, $I = n/6$: it grows with $n$ because each number is reused $n$ times, so a large GEMM is compute-bound. A $3 \times 3$ convolution with 64 channels reuses every weight at every pixel and lands far to the right as well.
maths.roof.machine: The chart uses this machine's numbers. The solid roofs are the best float32 GEMM rates measured on the BLAS tab of Coding Skills ({cpu} and {gpu}); the dotted lines above them are the theoretical peaks. Memory bandwidth was not measured: the slopes use nominal figures, 51.2 GB/s for the CPU (dual-channel DDR4-3200, assumed) and 484 GB/s for the GPU (vendor specification), so read the slopes as illustrative.
maths.roof.fusion: **Kernel fusion** moves memory-bound work to the right. `y = torch.relu(a * x + b)` run step by step launches three kernels, and each reads its input from memory and writes its output back: $6n$ numbers moved for $3n$ FLOPs. Fused into one kernel, which is what `torch.compile` does, $x$ is read once and $y$ written once: $2n$ numbers for the same $3n$ FLOPs, three times the intensity and, for a memory-bound kernel, up to three times the speed. GEMM gains nothing from this; it is already limited by arithmetic.
maths.roof.example: A float32 dot product of two vectors of $10^7$ numbers reads 80 MB and does $2 \times 10^7$ FLOPs. At 51.2 GB/s the reading alone takes about 1.6 ms, so the best possible rate is about 13 GFLOP/s, whatever the chip's peak. A $2048 \times 2048$ GEMM does $1.7 \times 10^{10}$ FLOPs on 50 MB: $I \approx 341$ FLOP/byte, far to the right of the ridge, so it can run close to the roof.
maths.roof.caption: Roofline of this machine (log–log). Dots: where each kernel sits for the chosen size; drag the slider to watch GEMM move right as $n$ grows.
maths.recap.title: Recap, and common misconceptions
maths.recap.kid: **Explain it to a 12-year-old.** A tensor is a box of numbers with labelled sides. Multiplying tensors means lining up one side of one box with one side of another, multiplying the numbers that meet and adding them up. Penrose drew the boxes as blobs with strings: tie two strings together and you have done that multiply-and-add. Which strings you tie first can make the job ten times shorter. And a computer is a chef with a slow delivery van: some jobs leave the chef waiting for ingredients, others keep the chef busy, and the roofline tells you which is which.
maths.recap.mis1: **"A tensor is just a multidimensional array."** In code, yes. In physics the tensor is the object behind the array, and the array is its components in one coordinate system. That is why stress is a tensor and an arbitrary table of numbers is not.
maths.recap.mis2: **"Rank means matrix rank."** Two different things share the word: the rank (order) of a tensor counts its indices; the rank of a matrix counts its independent rows. A $1000 \times 1000$ matrix always has tensor rank 2, but its matrix rank can be 1.
maths.recap.mis3: **"The order of multiplication does not matter."** For the result (associativity), it does not; for the cost, it matters enormously, as section 4 shows.
maths.recap.mis4: **"A faster GPU makes every kernel faster."** Only compute-bound ones. A memory-bound kernel runs at the speed of memory; more FLOP/s cannot help it, while fusion or better reuse of data can.
maths.recap.mis5: **"Upper and lower indices are only notation."** In curved space or with slanted axes they transform differently and the metric is needed to turn one into the other; with perpendicular unit axes in flat space they coincide, the only case array code deals with.
maths.recap.test: **The Feynman test.** If you can draw the Penrose picture of $\operatorname{tr}(ABC)$, write its `einsum` string, say which contraction order is cheapest for given shapes, and guess whether it will be memory- or compute-bound, you have understood this page.

history.gauss.title: Gauss's Remarkable Theorem
history.gauss.alt: Carl Friedrich Gauss, portrait by Christian Albrecht Jensen, 1840
history.gauss.p1: In 1827 Carl Friedrich Gauss, who was also leading the land survey of the Kingdom of Hanover, presented his "Disquisitiones generales circa superficies curvas" in Göttingen. Its **Theorema Egregium**, the "remarkable theorem", says that the curvature $K$ of a surface can be computed from lengths measured inside the surface alone, from the coefficients of $ds^2 = E\,du^2 + 2F\,du\,dv + G\,dv^2$, without ever looking at the space around it.
history.gauss.p2: An ant that never leaves its sphere can still find out that the sphere is curved. And no map of the Earth can be both flat and true to scale, because bending a surface leaves $K$ unchanged while flattening a sphere would not. Here the central idea of the tensor first appears: geometry is a small table of numbers at every point, and what matters is what stays the same when the coordinates change.
history.riemann.title: Riemann's lecture: geometry in n dimensions
history.riemann.p1: On 10 June 1854 Bernhard Riemann gave his Habilitation lecture in Göttingen, "Über die Hypothesen, welche der Geometrie zu Grunde liegen" (On the hypotheses which lie at the foundations of geometry). He had proposed three topics; by custom the first would be chosen, but the 77-year-old Gauss picked the third, the foundations of geometry, and Riemann had to prepare it.
history.riemann.p2: The lecture has almost no formulas, yet it lays out the whole programme: a space of any number $n$ of dimensions whose geometry is fixed by a line element that may change from point to point, in today's notation $ds^2 = g_{ij}\,dx^i dx^j$, and a curvature that measures how far it is from flat. According to Dedekind, Gauss left deeply impressed. The curvature tensor itself appears in Riemann's 1861 Paris prize essay; in $n$ dimensions it has $n^2(n^2-1)/12$ independent components, 1 for a surface and 20 for spacetime. The lecture was printed only in 1868, two years after Riemann's death.
history.christoffel.title: Christoffel's symbols
history.christoffel.alt: Elwin Bruno Christoffel, portrait from the ETH Library
history.christoffel.p1: When the coefficients $g_{ij}$ change from point to point, the ordinary derivative of a vector field depends on the coordinates you happen to use. In 1869 Elwin Bruno Christoffel, until that year a professor at the Zurich Polytechnikum, asked when two quadratic differential forms can be transformed into each other, and in Crelle's Journal introduced the three-index symbols now named after him: $\Gamma^k_{ij} = \tfrac12 g^{kl}(\partial_i g_{jl} + \partial_j g_{il} - \partial_l g_{ij})$.
history.christoffel.p2: They are not a tensor themselves; they are exactly the correction that turns a derivative into a covariant one. From them Christoffel built a four-index expression equivalent to Riemann's curvature, and his rule for deriving new invariants from old ones is what Ricci would later call covariant differentiation. In 1912 Grossmann would point Einstein to this very paper.
history.ricci.title: Ricci's absolute differential calculus
history.ricci.p1: In Padua, Gregorio Ricci-Curbastro spent roughly 1884 to 1894 turning these ideas into a system, set out in papers between 1888 and 1892. He called it the absolute differential calculus: absolute because its results do not depend on the coordinates. Upper (contravariant) and lower (covariant) indices record how a quantity transforms, contracting an upper with a lower index gives something coordinate-free, and the covariant derivative $\nabla_k$ carries those rules through differentiation.
history.ricci.p2: It was the whole toolbox of tensors, without the word "tensor". For years it found few users: many geometers preferred pictures to pages of indices, and the style was later mocked as "index gymnastics". Élie Cartan is often said to have complained of "débauches d'indices" (a debauch of indices), though no exact source for the phrase is known. As the MacTutor biography puts it, the importance of Ricci's work was not fully understood when he produced it.
history.methodes.title: Ricci and Levi-Civita: the "Méthodes"
history.methodes.alt: Felix Klein, who asked for the 1900 paper
history.methodes.p1: In Göttingen Felix Klein wanted an account of the method that the wider mathematical world would read, and around 1895 he asked Ricci for one. It appeared in 1900 in Mathematische Annalen, volume 54, written with Ricci's former student Tullio Levi-Civita: "Méthodes de calcul différentiel absolu et leurs applications", 77 pages applying the calculus to geometry, mechanics and mathematical physics.
history.methodes.p2: For more than a decade few physicists opened it. Then a Zurich mathematician, looking for the right tool for a friend, would find it. Part I ends here: the mathematics of curved spaces of any dimension is ready, waiting for a physical problem that needs it.
history.voigt.title: Voigt names the tensor
history.voigt.p1: The word came from physics, not geometry. In his 1898 book on the fundamental physical properties of crystals, the Göttingen physicist Woldemar Voigt used "tensor" in roughly today's sense, for the quantities of elasticity, stress and strain, which describe how a material is pulled (Latin tendere, to stretch) differently in different directions. William Rowan Hamilton had used the word in 1846 for something else: the length of a quaternion.
history.voigt.p2: The idea of stress as a table of numbers is older still. In the 1820s Augustin-Louis Cauchy described it for continuous media with nine numbers $\sigma_{ij}$, so that the force per unit area on any face with unit normal $n$ is $t_j = \sigma_{ij} n_i$. Voigt gave the family its name, and it stuck when Einstein and Grossmann used it in 1913 for the objects of the absolute differential calculus.
history.minkowski.title: Minkowski: space and time become one
history.minkowski.alt: Hermann Minkowski, frontispiece of "Raum und Zeit" (1909)
history.minkowski.p1:
On 21 September 1908 in Cologne, Hermann Minkowski opened his lecture "Raum und Zeit" with (in translation): "Henceforth space by itself, and time by itself, are doomed to fade away into mere shadows, and only a kind of union of the two will preserve an independent reality." Earlier that year he had rewritten electrodynamics in four dimensions: the electric and magnetic fields become one antisymmetric object, today's field tensor $F_{\mu
u}$, and Maxwell's equations shrink to $\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u} = \mu_0 J^
u$ and $\partial_{[\lambda} F_{\mu
u]} = 0$.
history.minkowski.p2: Einstein, once his student at the ETH, was at first unimpressed; he is reported to have called the four-dimensional rewriting "superfluous learnedness" (überflüssige Gelehrsamkeit). Within four years he would need far more of it than Minkowski had offered. Minkowski did not see it: he died suddenly in January 1909, aged 44.
history.grossmann.title: "Grossmann, you must help me"
history.grossmann.p1: Einstein's principle of equivalence (1907) said that gravity and acceleration cannot be told apart locally. By the summer of 1912 he had realised that gravity must be described by a variable metric $g_{\mu\nu}$, but he did not know the mathematics of such metrics. In August 1912 he returned to Zurich as professor at the ETH, where his old classmate Marcel Grossmann, whose lecture notes had once carried him through exams, was now professor of geometry.
history.grossmann.p2: As their colleague Louis Kollros recalled four decades later, Einstein pleaded: "Grossmann, Du musst mir helfen, sonst werd' ich verrückt!" (Grossmann, you must help me, or I'll go mad). It is a recollection, not a verbatim record. Grossmann searched the literature and found that the tools already existed: Christoffel, Ricci and Levi-Civita. On 29 October 1912 Einstein wrote to Sommerfeld that he had gained great respect for mathematics, "whose more subtle parts I considered until now, in my ignorance, as pure luxury".
history.entwurf.title: The "Entwurf": a near miss
history.entwurf.alt: Albert Einstein in 1912, photograph by Jan F. Langhans
history.entwurf.p1: In 1913 Einstein and Grossmann published "Entwurf einer verallgemeinerten Relativitätstheorie und einer Theorie der Gravitation" (Outline of a generalised theory of relativity and of a theory of gravitation). Einstein wrote the physical part, Grossmann the mathematical one. For the first time gravity was a metric tensor $g_{\mu\nu}$ with ten independent components, and matter entered through the energy–momentum tensor $T_{\mu\nu}$.
history.entwurf.p2: Einstein's research notebook of 1912–13, the "Zurich Notebook", shows that they examined field equations built from the Ricci tensor, very close to the final answer, and set them aside because they seemed not to give back Newton's law for weak fields and to clash with energy conservation. The Entwurf equations were therefore not generally covariant, and Einstein even devised the "hole argument" to convince himself that this was unavoidable. It cost him two years.
history.levicivita.title: Levi-Civita checks Einstein's mathematics
history.levicivita.p1: In the spring of 1915 Tullio Levi-Civita in Padua read Einstein's 1914 exposition of the Entwurf theory and wrote to say that a key step, Einstein's argument about the covariance of his gravitational equations, was wrong. The letters went back and forth between Padua and Berlin for weeks until Einstein conceded the error. By the autumn he had found further faults in the Entwurf equations and abandoned them.
history.levicivita.p2: In 1917 Levi-Civita gave the covariant derivative a geometric picture: parallel transport, the rule for carrying a vector along a curve in a curved space. That summer Einstein wrote to him, in an often-quoted letter, that it must be nice to ride through these fields "upon the horse of true mathematics" while people like himself had to make their way laboriously on foot (in translation; the English wordings vary).
history.field.title: November 1915: the field equations
history.field.alt: Albert Einstein lecturing in Vienna, 1921, photograph by Ferdinand Schmutzer
history.field.p1:
In November 1915 Einstein presented four papers to the Prussian Academy in Berlin in four weeks. On 18 November he showed that the new theory explains the 43 arcseconds per century of Mercury's perihelion advance that Newton's gravity could not; on 25 November he gave the final, generally covariant field equations. In today's form, $G_{\mu
u} = R_{\mu
u} - 	frac12 R\, g_{\mu
u} =  rac{8\pi G}{c^4} T_{\mu
u}$, or $G_{\mu
u} = 8\pi T_{\mu
u}$ in units with $G = c = 1$. David Hilbert reached the same equations from a variational principle at almost the same time.
history.field.p2: Spacetime tells matter how to move; matter tells spacetime how to curve, as John Wheeler later summed it up. In his 1916 review "Die Grundlage der allgemeinen Relativitätstheorie" Einstein also introduced a shorthand: an index that appears twice is summed, and the $\sum$ is no longer written. Every `einsum` still obeys this Einstein summation convention.
history.cuda.title: CUDA: a bet on programmable GPUs
history.cuda.alt: Board of a GeForce 8800 GTX, the first CUDA-capable GPU (2006)
history.cuda.p1: In November 2006 NVIDIA launched the GeForce 8800 GTX, its first GPU built from a unified array of programmable cores, and announced CUDA, a way to program them in C instead of disguising computations as graphics. The toolkit became public in 2007. Every GeForce sold, even to gamers who never used it, carried the extra hardware, so a lab could run matrix multiplications on a games card.
history.cuda.p2: It was an expensive bet. Jensen Huang later recalled that CUDA raised the company's costs by about 50% at a time when its gross margin was around 35%. In the 2008 crisis, on top of a large charge for defective laptop chips, NVIDIA's share price fell by more than 80% from its 2007 peak and the company reported losses, and investors questioned the spending for years. But the popular line that CUDA nearly bankrupted NVIDIA is an exaggeration: its real brush with failure came in 1996–97, before its first hit chip.
history.imagenet.title: ImageNet: data at the scale of the world
history.imagenet.alt: Fei-Fei Li speaking at AI for Good, 2017
history.imagenet.p1: Around 2007 Fei-Fei Li, then a young professor at Princeton, bet that what computer vision lacked was not cleverer algorithms but data. With Kai Li, the student Jia Deng and others she set out to illustrate the nouns of the WordNet hierarchy with hundreds of images each. Labelling by students would have taken decades, so the team turned to Amazon Mechanical Turk: between 2008 and 2010 almost 50,000 workers in 167 countries sorted the candidate images.
history.imagenet.p2: The first paper, at CVPR 2009, described 3.2 million images; the full ImageNet grew to about 14 million images in some 22,000 categories. As Li recounts in her memoir "The Worlds I See", grant applications were turned down and colleagues warned it was a risky use of a young career. From 2010 the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge used a 1,000-class subset with about 1.2 million training images: the benchmark that would make deep learning impossible to ignore.
history.alexnet.title: AlexNet: two gaming GPUs
history.alexnet.alt: A GeForce GTX 580 card with its cooler removed
history.alexnet.p1: Alex Krizhevsky, a PhD student of Geoffrey Hinton in Toronto, wrote cuda-convnet, his own CUDA code for convolutional networks, and with Ilya Sutskever trained an eight-layer network (60 million parameters, 650,000 neurons) on two GeForce GTX 580 cards with 3 GB each, splitting the network between them. Training took five to six days, by Hinton's later telling on a computer in Krizhevsky's bedroom at his parents' house.
history.alexnet.p2: At ILSVRC 2012 it reached a top-5 error of 15.3%; the next best entry had 26.2%. Every layer was a tensor operation: convolutions, ReLUs and matrix multiplications over batches of images. After this, computer vision, and soon the rest of AI, moved to deep networks on GPUs. In 2025 the Computer History Museum, together with Google, published the original source code.
history.cudnn.title: cuDNN: the primitives in one library
history.cudnn.alt: A convolution lowered to a matrix multiplication (GEMM)
history.cudnn.p1: By 2014 every lab was writing its own GPU convolution kernels. NVIDIA's cuDNN (Chetlur et al., 2014) packaged the primitives of deep learning, convolution, pooling, normalisation and activations, as tuned library calls on 4-D tensors in layouts such as NCHW (batch, channels, height, width).
history.cudnn.p2: Its main strategy lowers a convolution to a matrix multiplication (GEMM) without ever building the full unrolled matrix in memory; later versions added FFT and Winograd algorithms. Caffe, Theano and Torch adopted it quickly, and from then on the speed of a deep-learning framework largely meant the speed of a handful of tensor kernels: the same lesson as BLAS in the Coding Skills page.
history.tensorflow.title: TensorFlow: the name says it
history.tensorflow.alt: Tensors flowing through a dataflow graph
history.tensorflow.p1: On 9 November 2015 Google open-sourced TensorFlow, the successor of its internal DistBelief system. A program was a dataflow graph: nodes are operations and edges carry tensors, multidimensional arrays, and the graph could be placed on CPUs, GPUs and later TPUs, across many machines. Tensors, flowing through a graph.
history.tensorflow.p2: The tensor of deep learning is mostly the array of numbers rather than the geometric object with its transformation rules; but the habit of naming axes and contracting them is Ricci's. TensorFlow 2 (2019) made eager execution the default, partly in answer to PyTorch.
history.tpu.title: TPU: a systolic array for matrices
history.tpu.p1: In May 2016 Google revealed that since 2015 it had been running its own chip in its data centres: the Tensor Processing Unit. The 2017 ISCA paper by Norman Jouppi and colleagues described its heart, the Matrix Multiply Unit: a 256 × 256 systolic array of 65,536 8-bit multiply–accumulate cells. Weights stay in the cells while activations flow through them in waves, so every value fetched from memory is reused many times.
history.tpu.p2: The first TPU did inference only, with a peak of 92 trillion operations per second; on Google's own workloads it was on average about 15 to 30 times faster than the contemporary CPU and GPU, and 30 to 80 times better in performance per watt. Later generations added training and the bfloat16 floating-point format. The picture shows a TPU v3 board.
history.nvlink.title: NVLink and NVSwitch: many GPUs as one
history.nvlink.alt: The Tesla P100 (GP100) chip with its HBM2 memory stacks
history.nvlink.p1: Large models outgrew one GPU, and the PCIe bus became the bottleneck. NVIDIA announced NVLink in 2014; it first shipped in 2016 in the Tesla P100 (Pascal), whose four links gave up to 160 GB/s of bidirectional bandwidth to other GPUs, about five times a PCIe 3.0 ×16 slot. The P100 also put stacked HBM2 memory right next to the chip, as in the picture.
history.nvlink.p2: In 2018 NVSwitch turned point-to-point links into a switch fabric: in the DGX-2, twelve switch chips let 16 V100 GPUs talk to each other at full NVLink speed. Later generations scaled the idea to whole racks, with 72 GPUs in one NVLink domain in 2024's GB200 NVL72. For tensor programs this is what makes it practical to split one huge matrix multiplication across many GPUs and add up the pieces with an all-reduce.
history.dgx1.title: DGX-1 goes to OpenAI
history.dgx1.p1: In April 2016 NVIDIA announced the DGX-1: eight P100 GPUs joined by NVLink in one box, with a list price of 129,000 US dollars. On 15 August 2016 Jensen Huang personally delivered the first unit to OpenAI, then a young non-profit lab in San Francisco, signed with "I present you the world's first DGX-1!".
history.dgx1.p2: OpenAI's Ilya Sutskever said it would shorten experiments by weeks. OpenAI later scaled to thousands of GPUs, and the language models that followed are, at heart, enormous chains of the same tensor contractions as in Part I, running on hardware descended from that box.
history.pytorch.title: PyTorch: tensors you can print
history.pytorch.alt: Operations recorded on a tape, then differentiated backwards
history.pytorch.p1: At Facebook AI Research, Adam Paszke (then an intern), Sam Gross, Soumith Chintala and Gregory Chanan rebuilt the Lua-based Torch for Python; the first public release came in January 2017. Instead of building a graph first and running it later, PyTorch runs each operation at once (define-by-run, an idea it shared with Chainer) and records it on a tape for automatic differentiation. You could debug a network with `print()`.
history.pytorch.p2: Researchers moved over in large numbers; the 2019 NeurIPS paper describes the design. In 2022 PyTorch moved to the vendor-neutral PyTorch Foundation under the Linux Foundation. Its core object, `torch.Tensor`, is what every problem on this site computes with.
history.v100.title: Volta V100: Tensor Cores
history.v100.alt: A Tensor Core computes $D = AB + C$ on $4 \times 4$ tiles
history.v100.p1: In May 2017 NVIDIA announced the Volta V100: 21.1 billion transistors on an 815 mm² die and, for the first time, 640 Tensor Cores. Each Tensor Core performs a small matrix multiply–accumulate, $D = AB + C$ on $4 \times 4$ matrices, every clock cycle, with FP16 inputs and products accumulated in FP16 or FP32. Together they deliver up to 125 teraFLOPS for deep learning.
history.v100.p2: Tensor Cores are dedicated matrix multiply–accumulate units inside each streaming multiprocessor, fed by warps of threads; unlike the TPU's Matrix Multiply Unit they are not a large systolic array. Libraries such as cuBLAS and cuDNN use them when shapes and data types allow, which is why mixed precision (16-bit inputs, 32-bit accumulation) became the standard way to train.
history.m1.title: Apple M1: one memory for everything
history.m1.alt: Illustration of the Apple M1 package with its two memory chips
history.m1.p1: In November 2020 Apple introduced the M1, its first chip for the Mac: 16 billion transistors on a 5 nm process, with CPU, GPU and a 16-core Neural Engine (up to 11 trillion operations per second) on one die, and the memory in the same package. In this unified memory architecture all of them work on the same buffers, so a tensor does not have to be copied between CPU memory and GPU memory.
history.m1.p2: The CPU cluster also contains an undocumented matrix coprocessor, known as AMX (present since the A13 phone chip), which independent researchers have reverse-engineered and which Apple exposes through its Accelerate framework. Since PyTorch 1.12 (2022) the `mps` device runs tensors on the M-series GPU, one reason this site runs natively on Macs.
history.einsum.title: Finale: one line, a century-long relay
history.einsum.alt: The contraction $C_{ik} = A_{ij} B_{jk}$ written as `einsum("ij,jk->ik", A, B)`
history.einsum.p1: Today, when you write `torch.einsum("ij,jk->ik", A, B)`, you call on a relay that has run for almost two centuries: Gauss's insight that geometry can be measured from inside, Riemann's metric, Christoffel's symbols, Ricci's indices, Einstein dropping the $\sum$, and then GPUs, datasets, Tensor Cores, systolic arrays and NVLink that carry out the same contraction $C_{ik} = A_{ij} B_{jk}$ billions of times a second.
history.einsum.p2: On the Coding Skills page, the index contractions this story has followed (dot products, matrix products, sums over a shared index, even the Lorentz transformation of Minkowski's field tensor, `torch.einsum("ma,nb,ab->mn", L, L, F)`) are each written as one line of einsum. A notation invented for curved spacetime turned out to be the language of machines that learn.
nvlink.title: NVLink & NVSwitch: principles and programming
nvlink.intro: A model too large for one GPU has to split its tensors over several GPUs, and then every training step also moves tensors between them. NVLink is NVIDIA's direct GPU-to-GPU link; NVSwitch is the switch chip that joins many GPUs over NVLink. This tab explains why they exist, how fast each generation is, how GPUs are wired together, which collective operations run over the links, and how PyTorch uses them through NCCL.
nvlink.howto: Bandwidths are in GB/s ($1\ \text{GB} = 10^9$ bytes). NVIDIA quotes NVLink bandwidth per GPU with **both directions added** (bidirectional); one transfer from GPU A to GPU B gets at most half of it. Every table column says which of the two it shows, and every number links to the NVIDIA, NCCL or PyTorch document it comes from.
nvlink.why.title: Why GPUs need a fast interconnect
nvlink.why.text: Inside one GPU, tensors stream from HBM memory at terabytes per second. Between GPUs, the classic path is the PCIe bus, which is more than 20 times slower than the GPU's own memory. When a training step has to exchange gigabytes between GPUs, that link, not the arithmetic, sets the pace. NVLink closes most of the gap: on an H100, NVLink 4 moves 900 GB/s per GPU, which NVIDIA quotes as over 7 times PCIe Gen5.
nvlink.why.bar.caption: One H100 SXM GPU: PCIe Gen5 x16 (128 GB/s) and NVLink 4 (900 GB/s) with both directions added, and the GPU's own HBM3 memory bandwidth (3,350 GB/s). Fixed axis from 0 to 3,500 GB/s.
nvlink.why.timeTitle: Where multi-GPU training spends its communication time
nvlink.why.dp: **Data parallel.** Every GPU holds the whole model and a slice of the batch. After `backward()` the gradients of all GPUs are summed with an **all-reduce**: every step moves about twice the gradient size per GPU (2 bytes per parameter in bf16, so about 2 GB of gradients for a 1-billion-parameter model).
nvlink.why.tp: **Tensor parallel.** One layer's weight matrices are split over GPUs (columns on one, rows on another), so each layer ends with an all-reduce or all-gather of **activations**, in the forward and in the backward pass. This traffic sits on the critical path of every layer, which is why tensor parallelism is kept inside an NVLink domain.
nvlink.why.pp: **Pipeline parallel.** Consecutive layers live on different GPUs and only the activations at a stage boundary are sent, point to point, to the next GPU. Less data than tensor parallel, but GPUs wait for each other (the pipeline "bubble"), so a fast link still shortens each hand-over.
nvlink.gens.title: NVLink generations
nvlink.gens.text: Each generation either added links per GPU or made each link faster. From NVLink 2 to NVLink 4 one link carried 25 GB/s in each direction and the GPU got more links (6, 12, 18); NVLink 5 doubled the per-link rate. PCIe x16 doubled per generation too, but from a much lower start.
nvlink.gens.table.title: NVLink 1 to 5 and PCIe Gen3 to Gen6 x16: links and bandwidth per GPU
nvlink.gens.table.note: NVLink 1 and NVLink 5: NVIDIA states 40 GB/s and 100 GB/s per link with both directions added; the one-direction column is half of that. PCIe Gen3 and Gen4 x16 carry 15.75 and 31.5 GB/s in each direction (often rounded to 16 and 32); Gen5 carries 64 GB/s each way (128 GB/s total) and Gen6 256 GB/s total. P100 memory: 732 GB/s in the Volta whitepaper (the P100 overview rounds to 720).
nvlink.gens.card: {links} links × {perDir} GB/s per direction = {total} GB/s per GPU (both directions); memory {mem} GB/s
nvlink.gens.cardPcie: {perDir} GB/s per direction, {total} GB/s both directions
nvlink.topo.title: Topologies: mesh, switch and rack
nvlink.topo.text: A GPU has a fixed number of NVLinks, so how the links are wired decides who can talk to whom at full speed. With **point-to-point links** (a mesh) each GPU reaches only its direct neighbours; any other pair either takes two hops or falls back to PCIe. With an **NVSwitch** every GPU connects its links to switch chips, and every pair of GPUs talks at the GPU's full NVLink bandwidth, all at the same time (all-to-all).
nvlink.topo.svg.switchHops: GPU 0 → GPU 5: 1 hop via the switch
nvlink.topo.svg.caption: Left: 8 GPUs with 4 NVLinks each (16 links): two fully connected groups of 4 (front and back face of the cube, with diagonals) plus one link from each GPU to its partner in the other group. GPU 0 and GPU 5 share no link, so their data goes via GPU 4 (amber). Right: every GPU's links go to the NVSwitch (drawn as one box; real systems use several switch chips), so every pair is one hop apart at full bandwidth.
nvlink.topo.dgx1.tip: 2016 · 8 × Tesla P100 · 4 NVLinks per GPU · hybrid cube-mesh
nvlink.topo.dgx1.text: The first DGX-1 (2016) joined eight Tesla P100 GPUs with NVLink in a **hybrid cube-mesh**, the left diagram. The V100 version kept the same topology with 6 links per GPU. Fast inside each group of four, but collectives must be routed around the cube.
nvlink.topo.dgx2.tip: 2018 · 16 × V100 32 GB · 12 NVSwitches (6 per board) · 18 NVLink ports per switch at 51.5 GB/s · 2.4 TB/s bisection bandwidth
nvlink.topo.dgx2.text: **NVSwitch** (2018) is a switch chip with 18 NVLink ports. The DGX-2 used twelve of them, six on each of two boards, to join 16 V100 GPUs so that any GPU reaches any other at full NVLink bandwidth: 2.4 TB/s of bisection bandwidth. The later 8-GPU HGX boards (A100, H100, B200) also use NVSwitch, as in the right diagram.
nvlink.topo.nvl72.tip: Hopper: NVLink Switch System up to 256 GPUs · GB200 NVL72: 72 Blackwell GPUs in one NVLink domain, 1.8 TB/s per GPU, 130 TB/s in total
nvlink.topo.nvl72.text: The **NVLink Switch System** takes NVSwitch out of the box: switch trays connect GPUs in different servers over NVLink. NVIDIA describes up to 256 GPUs for Hopper; the **GB200 NVL72** rack puts 72 Blackwell GPUs into one NVLink domain with 130 TB/s of total NVLink bandwidth, so tensor parallelism can span a whole rack.
nvlink.topo.geforce.tip: RTX 2080 / 2080 Ti: NVLink bridge · RTX 3090 / 3090 Ti: NVLink (SLI-ready): Yes · RTX 4090: NVLink (SLI-ready): No
nvlink.topo.geforce.text: **Consumer cards** are different: no NVSwitch, at most a two-card NVLink bridge. NVIDIA lists the bridge for the GeForce RTX 2080 and 2080 Ti and NVLink for the RTX 3090 / 3090 Ti; the RTX 4090 specification says NVLink: No. Multi-GPU work on such cards goes over PCIe.
nvlink.coll.title: Collectives: what happens to the tensors
nvlink.coll.text: Multi-GPU programs rarely send single messages; they call **collectives**, operations in which all $N$ GPUs take part and each ends with a defined piece of the result. Below, $S$ is the size of the full tensor; the last column is how many bytes each GPU must send, as a multiple of $S$, with the bandwidth-optimal ring algorithm (NCCL's "bus bandwidth" factor).
nvlink.coll.allreduce.name: All-reduce
nvlink.coll.allreduce.what: Element-wise sum (or max, ...) of the tensors of all GPUs; every GPU gets the whole result. Used for gradient averaging in data parallel training.
nvlink.coll.allgather.name: All-gather
nvlink.coll.allgather.what: Every GPU contributes one slice; every GPU gets all slices concatenated. Used to rebuild sharded weights (FSDP, ZeRO).
nvlink.coll.reducescatter.name: Reduce-scatter
nvlink.coll.reducescatter.what: Sum over the GPUs like all-reduce, but GPU $i$ keeps only slice $i$ of the result. Used for sharded gradients (FSDP, ZeRO).
nvlink.coll.broadcast.name: Broadcast
nvlink.coll.broadcast.what: One GPU (the root) sends its tensor to all others. Used for the initial weights, so every replica starts the same.
nvlink.anim.start: Start: GPU i holds its own vector, split into 4 chunks
nvlink.anim.rs: Reduce-scatter, step {k} of {n}: send one chunk to the right neighbour, add it
nvlink.anim.ag: All-gather, step {k} of {n}: pass the finished chunks on, copy them
nvlink.anim.done: Done: every GPU holds the full sum Σ = a+b+c+d of every chunk
nvlink.anim.caption: Ring all-reduce on 4 GPUs holding the vectors a, b, c, d, each cut into 4 chunks (rows 0 to 3). In every step each GPU sends one chunk to its right neighbour (amber arrows; the last GPU wraps round to GPU 0). After $N-1 = 3$ reduce-scatter steps each GPU owns one fully summed chunk; $3$ all-gather steps then copy those chunks round the ring. Each GPU sent $2(N-1) = 6$ chunks of size $S/N$, that is $\tfrac{2(N-1)}{N}S$, and all links were busy in every step.
nvlink.coll.eqText: $S$: bytes to reduce, $N$: GPUs, $B$: link bandwidth in one direction (bytes/s), $\alpha$: fixed latency per step. For large tensors the bandwidth term dominates, and it hardly grows with $N$: the factor $\tfrac{2(N-1)}{N}$ goes from 1 (2 GPUs) to almost 2. That is why the ring is called bandwidth-optimal. Its weakness is the latency term, which grows linearly with $N$.
nvlink.coll.tree: A tree reduces up to a root and broadcasts back down, so it needs only about $2\log_2 N$ steps instead of $2(N-1)$. NCCL 2.4 added **double binary trees**, which keep the full bandwidth while their latency grows logarithmically; NVIDIA measured up to 180 times faster all-reduce than rings at 24,000 GPUs on the Summit supercomputer. For large messages on a few GPUs the ring is as good, and NCCL switches back to rings where they give more bandwidth.
nvlink.coll.ncclTitle: How NCCL picks NVLink, PCIe or the network
nvlink.coll.nccl: NCCL (the NVIDIA Collective Communications Library, PyTorch's GPU backend) detects the topology when the process group starts: which GPUs share NVLink or NVSwitch, which only share a PCIe switch or CPU socket, and which network cards (InfiniBand, RoCE, Ethernet) sit near which GPU. It then builds rings and trees over the fastest paths (inside a server over NVLink or PCIe peer-to-peer, between servers over the network) and chooses the algorithm per message size (`NCCL_ALGO`: Ring, Tree, and newer ones such as NVLS on NVSwitch systems). You normally leave all of this automatic; environment variables such as `NCCL_ALGO` and `NCCL_P2P_DISABLE` exist for experiments and debugging.
nvlink.code.title: Programming: PyTorch, NCCL and the tools
nvlink.code.text: In PyTorch you rarely touch NVLink directly: `torch.distributed` with the `nccl` backend runs the collectives, NCCL routes them over NVLink when it is there, and `torchrun` starts one process per GPU. The same script works on a PCIe-only machine, only slower.
nvlink.code.shown: These examples are **shown, not run**: the machine that builds this site has a single GPU, so there is no NVLink to measure. Only the last, single-process example runs anywhere.
